questions.q: What is a Microsoft Sentinel incident?
options: An object that groups one or more related alerts that share common entities
A single raw log event before any analytics rule has run
A permanent record that can never be closed once created
A playbook that runs automatically with no analyst involvement
questions.explain: Sentinel's incident correlation groups related alerts, such as several alerts on the same account, into one incident rather than handing an analyst disconnected alerts.

questions.q: What are the four severity levels Sentinel assigns to an incident?
options: Informational, Low, Medium, High
Minor, Major, Critical, Fatal
Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
New, Active, Resolved, Archived
questions.explain: Severity is set by the analytics rule that generated the incident's alerts and ranges from Informational up to High.

questions.q: What does assigning an incident to yourself on the Incidents page accomplish?
options: It claims the incident so two analysts don't duplicate work on the same case
It automatically closes the incident with a verdict
It raises the incident's severity level
It deletes the underlying alerts from the workspace
questions.explain: Assignment is part of the queue workflow — it signals ownership so the same incident isn't worked twice.

questions.q: When an analyst closes an incident, what three verdicts can they record?
options: True Positive, False Positive, Benign Positive
Approved, Denied, Pending
Critical, High, Low
Open, Closed, Reopened
questions.explain: These are the same three triage outcomes from the earlier generic triage lesson, now recorded directly on the Sentinel incident.

questions.q: Why does working the queue by severity rather than strict arrival order actually limit dwell time?
options: A High-severity incident left waiting risks extra minutes of an active attacker operating undetected, which costs far more than an older Low-severity incident waiting a bit longer
Sentinel automatically deletes incidents that aren't worked in arrival order
Arrival order and severity always match, so it makes no practical difference
Severity only matters for incidents that have already been closed
questions.explain: A High-severity incident waiting ten extra minutes can mean ten more minutes of real attacker activity, while an older Low-severity incident waiting longer costs comparatively little.
